questions.title: On a motion to dismiss an indictment, what facts can the court consider and why is review de novo?
questions.question_body: The panel says sufficiency of an indictment is reviewed de novo and that the court must take the allegations as true (citing Fontenot). I'm confused about the boundary here. Can a district court consider extrinsic evidence (like trading records) to test sufficiency, or is it strictly limited to the four corners of the indictment? And why is the appellate standard de novo rather than abuse of discretion when the district court dismissed?

questions.title: How does the government prove a 'scheme to defraud' under § 1348 when victims received market-value securities?
questions.question_body: The opinion relies on Kousisis to say actual economic loss isn't required and that obtaining money or property can be the object even if victims get equivalent value. In a pump-and-dump, if followers bought at market price and later could resell, what exactly is the 'property' deprivation? Is it the cash they parted with at the moment of purchase regardless of resale, or must the government tie the cash transfer specifically to the defendants (as counterparties) rather than to the market generally?

questions.title: What distinguishes the rejected 'right-to-control' theory from the accepted 'fraudulent-inducement' theory here?
questions.question_body: The panel says this case is unlike Ciminelli because it's not about depriving victims of valuable economic information, but about inducing them to part with money. Factually, the indictment emphasizes misstatements about the defendants' positions and price targets. Those are 'information' too. What makes those allegations cross the line from 'valuable economic information' (not property) to fraudulent inducement to transfer money (property)? Is it the causal linkage to an actual purchase obligation?

questions.title: What counts as a 'material misrepresentation' in a social-media pump-and-dump: puffery vs. actionable lie?
questions.question_body: The indictment alleges posts 'misrepresenting their trading positions and the potential price of securities.' I understand lying about your current holdings or intent to sell could be material, but what about optimistic price targets or hype—could those be dismissed as puffery or opinion? Does § 1348 adopt the Rule 10b-5 materiality framework (reasonable investor standard), and how would that apply to casual tweets vs. formal statements?

questions.title: Does § 1348 borrow all the scienter elements from mail/wire fraud, or is there a securities-specific gloss?
questions.question_body: The court says § 1348 'borrows key concepts' from mail and wire fraud and uses the Evans/Greenlaw framework (scheme + intent to defraud). Is the required mens rea identical to mail/wire fraud (intent to deceive + intent to obtain money/property), or does the 'in connection with any security' language import anything akin to Rule 10b-5's scienter or reliance concepts? In prosecutions under § 1348, is investor reliance ever an element or just evidentiary?

questions.title: How do conspiracy (§ 1349) and aiding-and-abetting (§ 2) apply if some defendants didn’t personally sell or profit?
questions.question_body: The indictment charges conspiracy and substantive § 1348 counts with § 2. Suppose a defendant only posted misleading content but didn’t sell into the spike or directly receive funds from followers. Is it enough for conspiracy that he agreed to the scheme and took overt acts, even if he didn’t profit? For aiding and abetting, what level of participation and intent must be shown—does merely amplifying others’ posts qualify?

questions.title: Are the defendants’ social-media statements protected by the First Amendment, and how does the fraud exception operate here?
questions.question_body: The posts are speech. The opinion doesn’t address First Amendment issues, but are misrepresentations about holdings/intent and false price predictions categorically unprotected as fraudulent commercial speech, or does the government still need to show knowing falsity and materiality to avoid First Amendment problems? Does it matter that the speakers held themselves out as traders rather than issuers or analysts?

questions.title: Must the government show that the defendants sought to obtain the followers’ money specifically, or just 'someone’s' money?
questions.question_body: Kousisis emphasizes that obtaining the victim’s money or property must be an object of the scheme. In a pump-and-dump, trades clear through the market; the defendants may not know who their counterparties are, and followers may buy from other sellers. Is it sufficient that the object was to obtain money from market purchasers generally, or must the indictment tie the object of the fraud to obtaining money from the deceived followers in particular?
